e.t: This word means 1 and is also the name of the letter alpha. It functions as an indeclinable number or letter designation rather than describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 118:1. The available lexical meaning identifies its basic sense clearly, while the surrounding verse would determine why this numeral or letter designation appears there. Its meaning remains limited to the numerical or alphabetical designation provided by the word itself.

Addi, also rendered Aththi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears three times, referring to a named person in genealogical or family-list material. The name occurs twice in Numbers 26:25 and once in 1 Chronicles 6:6. Without the surrounding verse text, its personal identity and role cannot be explained further from the name alone.

This LXX proper name refers to an Akkaronite, rendered in the lexical gloss as “Akkarōnitēs” or “Akkaronitis.” It identifies a person or people associated with that name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 13:3. Since the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its specific reference in that verse cannot be explained further here; its lexical sense is the designation “Akkaronite.”

This noun means “shackle” or “chains”—something used to bind or restrain a person. It names a physical restraint rather than an action or inner feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:16, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s basic picture is clear: a person held fast by a binding device or chain.

This noun means “threshing floor,” the place where harvested grain was processed and separated from its husks. It refers to a physical agricultural site, not to the grain itself or to the act of threshing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 54 times, appearing in passages from Genesis through Sirach. Its use in references such as Ruth 3:2 and Exodus 22:28 reflects the ordinary biblical setting of a floor or place associated with threshing.

This adjective describes something that cannot be transferred, changed, or revoked. It points to a fixed condition or decision that remains in force rather than being passed to someone else or altered. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 3 Maccabees.5. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is firmness and permanence.

This Greek LXX verb means to depart or go away. It describes leaving a place or moving away from someone or something, whether the departure is sudden, deliberate, or simply part of a journey. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is consistent across several narrative settings. The surrounding verse determines who leaves and why, but the word itself focuses on the act of departing rather than on a particular emotional or spiritual motive.

The adjective means “like flowers; blooming.” It describes something with a flower-like appearance or freshness, bringing the image of blossoms into the sentence rather than naming a flower itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Exodus 28:34. That single occurrence supports a focused, descriptive sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what object is being described there.

This verb means “disagreeable to”: it describes something that is not agreeable or acceptable to a person. As a verb, it expresses the effect of an action, condition, or matter on someone rather than naming the person or thing itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 21:15. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely what is disagreeable in that occurrence.

This verb means “cleanse”: to make something clean by removing what defiles or soils it. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its precise force depends on what is being cleansed in the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within Job and Proverbs. The word therefore presents cleansing as a deliberate act of removing impurity, with the immediate context determining whether the cleansing is literal or figurative.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “cut off”: to remove something by cutting it away or separate it from what it was attached to. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, across Deuteronomy, Judges, 2 Samuel, and Psalms. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being cut off and the surrounding sentence.

gl: strip off the scalp in Scythian fashion
d: strip off the scalp in Scythian fashion

e.t: This verb means to strip off the scalp in Scythian fashion. It describes a specific method of removing the scalp, rather than a general act of cutting or removing hair. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs only once, in 4 Maccabees 10:7. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain how the action functions in that passage.

This verb means “tear away”: to pull something off or separate it forcefully. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 9:28. The basic meaning remains concise, while the surrounding verse would determine exactly what is being torn away and how the action functions in that sentence.

This noun means “architecture” or “workmanship”: it refers to skilled building or crafted work. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only twice, both in Exodus 35. The word therefore names a kind of practical skill or completed craft rather than an emotion, person, or abstract teaching. Its two occurrences are Exodus 35:32 and Exodus 35:35, but the precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This adjective means “not of iron.” It describes something by saying that iron is not its material or quality, rather than naming the object itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it appears once, in Wisdom 17:15. Because no verse text is provided here, the word’s exact force in that sentence must be understood from its surrounding context; its basic lexical sense remains a direct description of something not of iron.

gl: having no hope of safety; abandoned
d: having no hope of safety; abandoned

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something abandoned and having no hope of safety. It presents a condition of being left exposed, without rescue or secure protection. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 7:11; the word’s precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea is not merely difficulty, but a state marked by abandonment and the absence of expected safety.

Baithani, also given as “Vethani,” is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular named place or person in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available information does not establish which kind of name it is. The name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:43. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding verse and broader passage context.

The word means “barbarously,” describing how an action is carried out. As an adverb, it modifies an action or statement rather than naming a person, place, or thing. Its basic sense presents conduct as barbarous in manner. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:2; the available information identifies the word’s meaning but does not include the verse text needed to explain its specific force there.

Besi, also written Vesi, is a proper name. It identifies a named individual or place in the Greek Old Testament, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Nehemiah 7:23. Its precise reference there requires the surrounding verse and passage, so the name itself should not be given an added meaning beyond Besi or Vesi.

This LXX noun means a “shoot,” referring to new growth that springs from a plant, stem, or branch. It describes something that emerges and develops from an existing source. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scripture preserved in this corpus, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Kings, Chronicles, Ezekiel, Job, and Sirach. Its exact force in any verse depends on whether the surrounding passage is describing a plant, tree, or figurative growth.

This word is a proper name, given as “Bouthan” or “Vuthan.” It functions as a personal or place-name designation rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers 33, at Numbers 33:6 and Numbers 33:7. The available information identifies the name but does not establish from the name alone whether it refers to a person, location, or another named entity.

This is a proper name, given as “Gaibaa” and “Yevaa.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 2:49. Because the verse text is not included here, its specific referent must be determined from that passage. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the personal name itself, not as a general word with an abstract definition.

This Greek LXX noun refers to nativity—the birth or manner of birth of a person, family, or people. It can also point to a group’s origin or lineage, especially when Scripture identifies how a people came into being or traces their beginnings. The word occurs 56 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, with many uses in Genesis and genealogical material. Its precise emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and context.

This adjective means “legitimate,” describing something recognized as genuine, rightful, or properly belonging. It can identify a person, relationship, status, or thing as valid rather than false or unauthorized. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Sirach 7:18 and 3 Maccabees 3:19. The surrounding wording is needed to show exactly what is being described in either passage, but the central idea remains that of something genuine and properly recognized.

This adjective means “at the angle,” describing something located at or associated with a corner or angled point. It identifies position rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 38:6, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and context, but the central idea remains something situated at an angle or corner.

This verb means “steer through; govern.” It describes directing something safely or exercising oversight, like a helmsman guiding a vessel or a person managing an undertaking. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Wisdom and 3 Maccabees. The word therefore carries an active sense of guiding or administering rather than merely possessing authority. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is purposeful direction and control.

This word means “double burden; load,” describing something carried as a heavy or compounded responsibility. It is a noun, so it names the burden rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Judges 5:16, making it a rare word whose precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains a load that is doubled or unusually weighty.

This word means “Hebrew.” In the Greek Old Testament, it can identify a person as Hebrew or describe something as belonging to the Hebrews, depending on how it functions in the sentence. It is used 37 times in the LXX corpus, across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its basic sense remains an identity or description connected with being Hebrew, while the surrounding verse determines whether it refers to a person or a Hebrew-related designation.

This Greek LXX noun means “anger; hatred,” describing strong hostile feeling toward someone or something. It names an inward attitude rather than an action, so the surrounding passage determines how intense or directed that feeling is. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs once, in Jeremiah 31:39. Its English rendering there is “anger,” while the broader lexical sense also includes hatred. The word should therefore be understood as a settled or forceful hostile disposition, not merely a brief annoyance.

This LXX verb means “make to change one’s habits.” It describes an action that brings about a change in a person’s customary way of living or conduct. As a verb, it points to doing this, not simply naming a habit or a change. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument.

This Greek verb means to “seek out/thoroughly”—to search for someone or something with deliberate thoroughness. It describes active seeking rather than a casual glance or passing interest. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 128 times, showing that this is a well-used expression for pursuing, investigating, or looking carefully for what is sought. Its exact emphasis in a particular verse depends on what is being sought and the surrounding sentence.

This adjective means “sixteenth,” identifying a person, thing, or position that comes after the fifteenth and before the seventeenth. It is an ordinal number rather than a description of character or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Chronicles. Its exact reference—such as a numbered group, order, or place—depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself consistently marks the number sixteen in sequence.

gl: bring up from childhood; educate completely
d: bring up from childhood; educate completely

e.t: This verb means to “bring up from childhood” or “educate completely.” It describes the act of raising and thoroughly educating someone, emphasizing formation from an early age through full instruction. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 1:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is clear: to train or educate someone fully rather than merely give brief instruction.

Eliphaleth is a personal name, also rendered “Elifaleth.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 10:33. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its significance here is limited to identifying the person named. The spelling “Eliphaleth” is the primary rendering, while “Elifaleth” is another form of the same name.

This adjective describes something that is wanting or lacking—something incomplete because it does not have what is needed. It points to deficiency or absence rather than abundance or fullness. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in Sirach 14:10. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense remains a condition of lacking or falling short.

This noun means “indignation,” expressing strong anger or displeasure toward something regarded as wrong or offensive. It names an intense emotional response rather than an action or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Lamentations 2:6. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what or whom this indignation concerns, but the word itself points to forceful displeasure. Its concise meaning is therefore indignation: a serious, inward response of anger. [p03:word:lxx:L704554:identity; p03:word:lxx:L704554:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L704554:reference:0]

This verb means “put on”—to place something onto oneself or otherwise take it on. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: once each in 2 Samuel, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its exact object and significance depend on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains the act of putting on.

e.h: Take a Pledge or Give Security
e.t: This verb means to take a pledge or give security. It describes an action involving a pledge or assurance, functioning as a verb rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 24:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the taking of a pledge or the giving of security.

This Greek LXX verb means “put in”—to place something inside or into something else. It describes an action rather than an object, so its exact sense depends on what is being placed and where. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, appearing once each in Ezra, Proverbs, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its basic idea remains straightforward: someone puts, places, or inserts something in a particular location. The surrounding verse supplies the specific object and setting.

This adverb means “especially” or “above others,” marking someone or something as having a distinct or higher place compared with others. It adds emphasis to the word or idea it describes rather than naming an action or object by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:31. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its basic meaning is to single out one person, thing, or consideration as especially prominent.

This Greek LXX word means “upon” or “above.” It describes the position of one thing in relation to another, indicating that something is on top of, over, or higher than something else. It can also function as a preposition, connecting a noun or pronoun with the thing above or over it, or as an adverb describing location. The word occurs 119 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic spatial sense appears across many kinds of passages. The surrounding words determine its precise sense in any particular verse.

gl: flow upon the surface; float a-top
d: flow upon the surface; float a-top

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “flow upon the surface” or “float a-top.” It describes something moving or remaining on the upper surface of water or another substance, rather than sinking beneath it. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Job 22:16. Its basic sense is physical and describes surface movement; the surrounding verse is needed to determine the precise force of the word in that passage.

This LXX verb means to bring something upon someone or to conspire against them. It describes an action directed toward another person or group, especially when trouble, opposition, or a hostile purpose is involved. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including passages in Leviticus, Numbers, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Sirach. Depending on the sentence, it may emphasize causing something to happen to others or joining together in opposition against them.

This word means “sevenfold”. It describes something multiplied by seven or occurring seven times. As an adjective, it qualifies a person, thing, or action by expressing this sevenfold measure. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times across Proverbs, Isaiah, and Sirach. The word can therefore mark a complete multiplication or intensified amount, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is counted or multiplied. Its central idea remains a quantity or degree increased seven times.

This Greek verb means “explore” or “check.” It describes examining or searching something to discover what is present or to verify a matter. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 13 times, showing repeated use for investigative activity across several books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being examined, but the central idea remains active searching or checking.

This noun refers to “benevolence” or “satisfaction”—a disposition of goodwill, or a sense of approval and contentment. It can describe favorable purpose toward someone or the pleasure that comes from something being pleasing or accepted. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs 24 times, appearing especially in Sirach and Psalms. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on whether the surrounding sentence emphasizes goodwill toward others or satisfaction in an outcome or condition.

This adjective describes something that is well-based, well-built, or firmly established. It can refer to a person, structure, or arrangement whose stability and sound construction are being emphasized. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, in Esther, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its central idea is dependable solidity: something properly founded and not flimsy or poorly made. The exact object it describes must be identified from the surrounding verse, but the word itself points to strength, stability, and sound formation.

Zarai, also rendered Zare, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs six times, in Numbers, Joshua, and 1 Chronicles. Because no broader definition or thematic association is given, its meaning is chiefly its role as a proper name identifying an individual in genealogical and historical passages.

Ela, also rendered Ila, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies people in the Greek Old Testament, so its meaning is primarily its use as a name. This name occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, and 2 Kings. The specific person identified must be determined from the surrounding passage, since the name itself does not express that person’s character or role.

This word means “furnaces,” referring to enclosed places or structures used for intense heat, commonly for heating or processing materials. It is a noun naming such heating installations rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 3:11. The precise role of the furnaces there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself identifies furnaces as physical structures associated with heat.

This adjective describes something that is wished for or desired—something a person wants or regards as desirable. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only twice, so its basic sense is clear even though its particular force in each verse depends on the surrounding passage. It occurs in 1 Samuel 15:22 and Malachi 3:12. The word functions as a describing term rather than naming an action or person.

This Greek LXX noun means “religion,” referring to the practice or expression of religious devotion. It names religion as a recognizable way of honoring and serving a deity, rather than describing a person, place, or isolated action. The word occurs four times in the deuterocanonical Greek writings represented here: twice in Wisdom and twice in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains religion or religious practice. This word belongs to the Greek LXX corpus and should be understood within that corpus.

Iarmoth is a proper name in the Greek LXX, identifying someone or something named Iarmoth. Its exact referent—whether a person, place, or another named entity—cannot be determined from the lexical information alone, so the surrounding verse is needed for that distinction. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Ezra 10:27. It is not a general description or action word, but a specific name.

This proper noun identifies a Jezreelite, also rendered “Iezrelitis.” It functions as a personal or identifying designation connected with the people or place named Jezreel. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across eight verses, appearing in 1 Kings and 2 Kings. Its references are concentrated in 1 Kings 20 and continue through 2 Kings 9. The word itself supplies a designation rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept.

This Greek word describes someone as merciful or an action as favorably disposed, expressing compassion, graciousness, or a willingness to show favor. It can function as an adjective, adverb, or noun, so its exact English wording depends on how it is used in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, it occurs 35 times. Its central idea remains the same: mercy shown toward someone, or a favorable disposition toward a request or person.

Isei, also rendered Isi, is a personal name rather than a descriptive word or action. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles. The name itself identifies a person, but the available information does not provide an additional meaning or description attached to it. Its precise significance in either passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and family or historical context.

This noun refers to a misadventure or failure—a situation in which an undertaking goes badly or a person experiences an unsuccessful outcome. It names the unfortunate result itself rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 5:23. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense is an adverse outcome or failure. [Source: Wisdom 5:23]

This adverb means “strongly,” describing an action carried out with firmness or intensity. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:31. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what action it describes there, but its basic sense remains an emphatic manner of acting: with strength, firmness, or force.

This Greek LXX verb means “feed flocks upon,” describing the act of letting sheep or other flock animals feed on something. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within Exodus 22:4. The broader sense remains focused on providing or directing food for a flock, while the precise object being grazed depends on the sentence where the verb appears.

This verb means “grind down,” describing the action of reducing something through grinding. It presents a forceful process that wears material down rather than simply moving or breaking it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in Exodus, Deuteronomy, and Daniel. Its exact emphasis in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its object, but the central idea remains the thorough grinding down of something.

This Greek LXX verb means “break down,” describing something giving way, collapsing, or being brought down. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing once each in Joshua and Proverbs and twice in Psalms. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being described and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of breaking down or coming down.

This noun means a “round of a ladder,” the horizontal part that a person steps on when climbing. It names one of the ladder’s repeated crosspieces, so its meaning is concrete and architectural rather than figurative. In the Greek Old Testament translation, it occurs six times, all in Ezekiel’s description of the temple and its steps. The word therefore identifies a physical ladder step or rung in those passages.

This word means “tassel,” a hanging decorative or identifying element attached to clothing or fabric. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, appearing in Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Zechariah. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a tassel or attached hanging piece.

This verb means “act as pilot”: to perform the work of guiding or directing as a pilot. It describes someone carrying out a pilot’s role rather than merely possessing that position. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, in Proverbs and Wisdom, including references in Proverbs 12:5, Wisdom 10:4, and Wisdom 14:6. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

This word means “hewn out,” describing something shaped by cutting or carving. It functions as an adjective or noun, identifying an object made by being cut from a material rather than left in its natural form. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Kings, at 2 Kings 12:13 and 2 Kings 22:6. Its basic meaning remains focused on the result of workmanship: something cut out, carved, or fashioned by human labor.

This adjective describes something that pays what is due. It refers to fulfilling an obligation or settling what is properly owed. The word therefore focuses on the payment or fulfillment itself, not on a person’s title or identity. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 28:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX verb means “rave”: to speak or behave in a wildly uncontrolled way, often suggesting a loss of sound judgment. It describes an action rather than a person or object, telling what someone does. The word occurs four times in the LXX corpus, appearing in Jeremiah, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse context.

Mambrē, also rendered Mamvri, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named biblical entity and appears ten times, all in Genesis. The name is found from Genesis 13 through Genesis 50, including passages associated with Abraham and later with Joseph’s family history. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent in each occurrence cannot be explained further, but its basic function is clear: it is a personal or place name preserved as Mambrē.

This Greek adjective means “great” or “loud,” describing something large, strong, prominent, or notable, and in some contexts describing sound that is raised or powerful. It is a broad descriptive word rather than a title or technical term. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 732 times, so its precise force depends on the noun or action it describes. Its uses range across descriptions of people, things, events, and sounds, while retaining the central idea of greatness or intensity.

This Greek LXX verb means to follow closely after someone or to pursue them. It describes directed action: staying after a person in close pursuit rather than merely noticing or accompanying them. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 2:31. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of following closely or pursuing.

This Greek LXX noun means “participation” or “partnership”—sharing in something or having a part with others. It describes involvement or fellowship rather than merely observing from a distance. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 2:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is taking part together in something shared.

This word means “little” and functions as an adverb, describing something as small in degree or amount. It expresses a limited extent rather than a large or complete measure. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:8. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a small amount or limited degree.

Moab is a proper name referring to Moab in the Greek Old Testament. It is a specific biblical name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 164 times across 147 verses in the LXX corpus, from Genesis 19:37 through Zephaniah 2:9. Its repeated use across historical, legal, prophetic, and narrative books shows that Moab is a recurring named subject in the Old Testament. The precise significance of Moab in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding text.

Naana is a proper name referring to a person named Naana. It is not presented here as a general description, action, or quality, but as an individual’s name. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 8:7. The name’s precise significance beyond identifying that person is not established by the available lexical definition, so it is best understood simply as the personal name Naana.

This Greek LXX noun means “conquest”—the gaining of victory over an opposing person, people, or power. It points to the achieved triumph itself rather than describing the act of fighting as a process. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, appearing once in 2 Samuel and twice in the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “south wind.” It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament to name wind coming from the south and, in some settings, to identify the southern direction. The word appears 72 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including descriptions of boundaries, locations, and winds. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the south wind or what lies toward the south.

This Greek LXX verb means to entertain or to astonish. It can describe receiving or hosting someone, and it can also describe causing someone to react with wonder or surprise. The word appears four times in the LXX corpus, in Esther, Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes welcoming someone or producing astonishment.

This Greek LXX noun means “cell,” referring to a confined or enclosed space. It identifies a particular kind of room or compartment rather than an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Ezekiel and once in Wisdom. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the space. The basic meaning remains a cell: an enclosed place set apart for a specific purpose.

This LXX adverb means “real; really,” marking something as genuine or emphasizing that it truly is so. It strengthens a statement by drawing attention to reality or truth. The word occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in four Old Testament verses and one verse in Wisdom. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This adverb means “uprightly” or “normally.” It describes how an action is performed or how something is regarded: in a right, proper, or ordinary manner. The word appears 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is consistent while the surrounding sentence determines whether it points to proper conduct or what is usual. It does not name a person or object; it qualifies an action, judgment, or description.

This Greek LXX adverb means “long ago,” referring to something that happened or existed in the distant past. It points backward in time rather than describing an action, person, or place. The word appears eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including passages from Esther, Isaiah, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what past event or condition the surrounding words identify.

This word means “mad”: it describes someone acting in a state of madness or lacking sound judgment. As a verb, it expresses becoming or behaving mad rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Zechariah 7:11. That reference identifies its sole occurrence, while the word’s precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

“For mourning” or “mournful” describes something connected with grief and the outward expression of sorrow. As an adjective, the word characterizes a person, object, or appearance as suited to mourning rather than naming the act of mourning itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Exodus and once in 2 Samuel. Its central sense remains consistent: marked by grief or intended for a season of sorrow. The surrounding verse determines exactly what it describes in each passage.

This verb means to “burn round about,” describing burning that takes place around something rather than simply at one isolated point. Its basic sense focuses on the action itself and does not, by itself, explain the wider situation or purpose. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears only once, at 4 Maccabees 16:3, so its precise force there depends on the verse and surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to adornment or a robe—something worn as clothing or used to enhance appearance. Its central idea is an outward covering or decoration, rather than an action or inner quality. It occurs twice in the LXX corpus, once in Exodus and once in Sirach, showing its use for a tangible garment or adornment. The surrounding verse determines which aspect is emphasized.

This noun means “worker in clay,” referring to a person whose work involves shaping or handling clay. It identifies an occupation rather than an abstract quality or action. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 15:7. Its basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete: a clay worker. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the word’s particular role in that passage.

This adjective means “numerous,” describing a group or collection that contains many individuals or things. It emphasizes quantity rather than identity, quality, or importance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Deuteronomy 30:5 and 1 Maccabees 4:35. The surrounding words determine exactly what is numerous in each passage, but the central idea remains a large number or abundant company. Its use is straightforward: it adds the sense of many to the noun or subject it describes.

This word means “forerunner”: someone who goes ahead of others. It can function as a noun for such a person or as an adjective describing someone or something that comes beforehand. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, in Numbers, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its basic idea is priority in movement or arrival—the one who precedes others. The surrounding verse determines what the forerunner is doing or why that precedence matters.

This verb means to predict—to declare or indicate something before it happens. It describes the act of foretelling an event or outcome, rather than merely noticing or describing what is already present. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:19. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context. Its central idea remains clear: giving advance notice of what is expected to happen.

This verb means to “assume the first seat among,” describing someone taking the foremost place in a group. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it occurs once, in Esther 3:1. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact force in that occurrence must be understood from its context.

e.h: A Word for Bring Forth Her First Child
e.t: This word means “bring forth her first child”. It is a verb describing a first birth, and it can also refer to an animal calving for the first time. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Samuel and Jeremiah. Its references concern the basic act of bringing forth a first offspring, while the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “root”: the part of a plant that anchors it in the ground and supplies nourishment. By extension, a root can point to the underlying source or foundation from which something grows, though its exact sense depends on the sentence. It occurs 49 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages in Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Proverbs. The word is used for both physical roots and the foundational source of something.

Saarēm; Saarim is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:8. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is provided here, the name itself gives the main meaning: it identifies an individual. Its precise identity and significance must be understood from the genealogy and context in that passage.

Samsaria is a proper name, referring to a particular person or place identified by that name rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 8:26. Because it is a name, its ordinary meaning is its identifying designation; the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly whom or what Samsaria identifies there.

Saou, also rendered Sau, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 2:49. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s specific family or narrative role should be understood from that passage rather than inferred from the name itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “shake”: to move something forcefully or to tremble and be moved. It describes physical shaking and can be used wherever the surrounding sentence presents something as being shaken. The word occurs 34 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, so it is a recurring action word rather than a rare or specialized term. Its exact sense—whether someone shakes something or something shakes—depends on how it functions in the individual verse.

This word means “of you” or “your.” It is a pronoun that connects something with the person or people being addressed, expressing possession or association. For example, it can identify something belonging to you or connected with you. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 5,764 times, so it is a common way to express this relationship across many kinds of sentences. Its exact English wording depends on the noun or phrase it accompanies, but its central idea remains connection with the person addressed.

e.h: To Seed or Go to Seed
e.t: This verb means “go to seed” or “seed,” referring to producing or scattering seed. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Exodus 9:31 and Leviticus 12:2. Its basic sense belongs to the process of sowing or reproduction, depending on the sentence in which it occurs. The word therefore describes an action connected with seed, rather than naming the seed itself.

“Stoutly” means acting with firmness, strength, or determination. As an adverb, it describes how someone carries out an action rather than naming a person or thing. This Greek LXX word occurs once, in Habakkuk 2:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is resolute or forceful action. It should therefore be understood as describing the manner of an action: doing something stoutly.

This Greek LXX verb means “grieve altogether,” describing complete or deeply felt grief. It expresses the act of grieving rather than naming a person, object, or state. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Psalms and once in Isaiah, so its meaning is focused and specific rather than broadly varied across many passages. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a full experience or expression of grief.

“Fellow-drinker” or “boon-companion” describes a person who drinks with someone and is regarded as a companion in that setting. As a noun, the word identifies the person rather than the act of drinking. Its central idea is companionship joined to shared drinking, while the surrounding passage determines the particular tone or relationship intended. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 2:25.

This adjective describes something covered, darkened, or obscured by clouds—“clouded over; cloudy.” It portrays a sky or scene whose clarity is hidden beneath cloud cover, rather than something bright and clear. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Deuteronomy 33:28. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its ordinary meaning remains a description of cloudy or overcast conditions.

This Greek LXX noun means “ruin” or “crushing”—the condition or result of being broken down, overwhelmed, or brought to destruction. It describes severe damage or collapse rather than a person or action by itself. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in 2 Samuel, Jeremiah, Amos, Micah, and Zephaniah. Its precise force in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains ruin or crushing.

Tano is a proper name, rendered as “Tano” in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented as an ordinary descriptive word or action, but as the designation of a named entity. This word occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 15:34. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its specific referent cannot be identified here; its lexical role is simply a proper name preserved as Tano.

This Greek LXX verb means “devise” or “plan”: to form an intention or work out what one will do. It can describe thoughtful purposes, whether directed toward good or harmful ends, so the surrounding sentence determines the moral character of the plan. The word appears 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, with especially frequent use in Proverbs. It is an action word, focusing on the act of forming or arranging a purpose rather than merely having a passing thought.

This word means “four thousand,” expressing a specific numerical quantity. It functions as a number, usually describing or counting people, objects, or measurements. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, including several uses in Ezekiel 48 for measured dimensions. Its basic meaning remains numerical rather than symbolic: it identifies an amount of four groups of one thousand. The surrounding verse determines what is being counted or measured.

This word means “at that”. It is an adverb that points back to a time, event, or circumstance already mentioned, helping the reader understand when something happened or when a statement applies. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 225 times, showing that it is a regular way to connect one moment with what follows or with something previously described. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central function remains a simple reference to that earlier time or situation.

This word means “forest,” referring to a wooded area or collection of trees. It is a noun in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, where it can name a natural place or wooded material according to the surrounding sentence. The word occurs eight times in this Greek corpus, across books including Job, Isaiah, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a forest or woodland setting.

This Greek LXX noun means “meeting,” referring to an encounter or coming together. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Judges 11:34. The word itself identifies the gathering or encounter, while the surrounding verse and passage determine who is meeting and what the meeting involves. Its basic sense is therefore straightforward: a meeting, understood as people coming together in one place or for an encounter.

Pherezi is a proper name, also rendered “Ferezi.” It functions as a specific designation rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Ezra 9:1. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not establish its exact referent or role from the verse alone. Its significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding biblical text.

This noun means “corruption”: the condition or process of becoming spoiled, ruined, or subject to decay. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes deterioration rather than something sound and whole. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages rendered with “corruption.” Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains damage, decay, or ruin affecting what was previously intact.

This Greek LXX noun refers either to a prison, a place where people are held, or to a watch, a period or duty of guarding. Its meaning therefore depends on whether the sentence concerns confinement or vigilant protection. It occurs 117 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing that both senses are established uses rather than rare exceptions. It is rendered “prison” in Genesis 40:3 and “watch” in Exodus 14:24, illustrating these two basic meanings.

This word is the proper name “Olam,” functioning as a personal name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, at 1 Chronicles 26:3. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore the identification of someone named Olam, with the spelling also represented as Ōlam.
